📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Having grown up in the U.K., Sienna Spiro never got the chance to soak up the singular type of magic that permeates Manhattan in the lead-up to the holidays. So go figure that at 21 years old, she’d find herself slap bang in the middle of the buzz. On Friday evening, as crowds swarmed Lexington Avenue and 59th Street to catch a glimpse of the breakthrough singer, Spiro was on hand to unveil the Bloomingdale’s holiday windows, created this season in collaboration with Ralph Lauren.

“It’s my first time seeing Fresh York at Christmas. I didn’t even know this [opportunity] was an option. I’m so happy about it,” Spiro told Vogue in the greenroom ahead of the public performance. Even in the context of her “whirlwind” year, it had been quite the week: On Monday, she was revealed as a contender for Best New Artist at the 2027 Grammys, and on Wednesday, her name appeared on the lineup for next summer’s Glastonbury festival. “This year has been just insane,” she mentioned. “There’s no fancy word for it. Something new has happened every single day. I can’t really keep up with it to be honest.”.

For her latest surreal career moment, the rising star donned a glossy red mackintosh coat from the Ralph Lauren archives, which she paired with black leather driving gloves and sky-high Louboutins—very in keeping with her youthful spin on a vintage-esque look that has been keeping her fans enthralled.

Recent findings suggest that though she’s not typically swayed by traditional Christmas songs, Spiro thrilled the audience with her one exception: “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas.” “The Frank Sinatra version, of course, with a little saxophone solo,” she noted. Those who had dutifully lined up to hear her smoky tones in real life were delighted when she also launched into “Material Lover” and “Great Expectations.” Indeed, clips of the performance had already made it onto TikTok minutes after she departed the stage—fitting for a performer who was discovered on the platform as a teen.

Just after 7 p.m., Bloomingdale’s CEO Olivier Bron and Ralph Lauren chief branding and innovation officer David Lauren appeared to count down the window and lighting reveal. “We’re bringing two iconic New York brands together, who share the same appreciation for heritage, craftsmanship, and fashion,” Bron noted. Behind them, vignettes provided an instant immersion into the plaid- and velvet-drenched world of Ralph Lauren during the holidays.

Post-show, guests, many of whom were dressed in Ralph Lauren, headed back into the department store to see the extent of the festive programming. At Forty Carrots, an UGG takeover sees specialty frozen yogurt on offer, while Roberto Coin has teamed up with Studio 59 on a upcoming Italian menu. Around the store, which felt like an ode to a Love Actually scene, there was everything from a cappella trios and DJs to embroiderers busy at work personalizing presents.

Sources indicate that as for Spiro, who had spent the previous night “singing her heart out” when she got to meet her idol Stevie Wonder at Madison Square Garden, she’s doing the holidays a little differently this year, and is set to spend the break in Japan ahead of kickstarting her next tour there in January. “It’s my first time going. I told them I’d play in a Starbucks if I had to, I just really wanted to get there.” With three tours, numerous awards shows, and the festival circuit on the horizon, it’ll be a welcome chance to finally catch her breath.

In a recent development, “I’m really excited to just live a bit, outside of all of this, and grow,” she told Vogue. “I’m still super young. To be a really amazing artist, you’ve got to grow as a person so I’m excited to live, learn, and hopefully end up writing my next record at some point.”.

These Thanksgiving sandwiches make the most of what you’ve got, whether that’s a few slices of turkey or enough stuffing and cranberry sauce for an encore. Go all in with a gooey melt, load a pita with spiced turkey and crunchy vegetables, or give turkey the chicken salad treatment. Industry observers note that give your Thanksgiving leftovers the club treatment by layering turkey and cranberry sauce with crisp bacon and lettuce. And don’t forget that middle slide of bread. We’re not animals, after all.

Sources indicate that in this play on a turkey club, the middle slice of bread gets swapped out for leftover stuffing fried in bacon fat. (We repeat: stuffing fried in bacon fat.).

Industry observers note that turkey and cranberry sauce already have a salty-sweet thing going on. Why not play that up by swapping plain bread for custardy French toast?

Sometimes it’s best to keep a leftover turkey sandwich simple. Turkey, cranberry sauce, cheese, and fresh sage, pressed until golden, give you all the flavors of Thanksgiving in four ingredients (plus bread).

Industry observers note that though the recipe calls for cooked chicken, you guessed it—you can swap in leftover turkey seamlessly. The apple and fennel both provide lots of crunch and freshness.

This recipe sticks close to the classic turkey club, with one simple twist: a punchy, verdant herb mayo that comes together in seconds in the blender.

Place 10.5 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a large heatproof bowl. Bring 1 cup whole milk to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium, about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, vigorously whisk 4 large egg yolks and ½ cup (100 g) sugar in a small heatproof bowl until smooth and lemon yellow, about 1 minute.

According to recent reports, gradually stream hot milk into yolk mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Return to pan, scraping bowl clean with a heatproof rubber spatula. Cook over medium, stirring constantly, until thickened just enough to coat a spoon, about 5 minutes. (Do not let custard come to a boil or it will curdle.) Immediately pour over chocolate; let sit 1 minute. Add 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and whisk vigorously until chocolate is melted and crémeux is smooth.

In a recent development, beat 1¾ cups heavy cream in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until soft peaks form, about 5 minutes. Add one quarter of whipped cream to crémeux; mix until combined (this will lighten it). Add remaining whipped cream in 3 additions, gently folding after each until incorporated before adding more.

Reassemble springform pan; line bottom with a parchment paper round. Wrap a strip of parchment around inside of pan to create a collar that stands about 1" above band (ends should overlap by at least 3"). Using a large serrated knife, trim off mound on top of cake to create a flat surface if needed. Return cake to pan. Spoon mousse over and smooth into an even layer with an offset spatula or spoon. Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet; chill until top of mousse feels set, about 2 hours.

According to recent reports, place 4 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a medium heatproof bowl. Bring ½ cup heavy cream and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt to a bare simmer in a small saucepan over medium. Pour over chocolate and let sit 2 minutes. Whisk gently until smooth. What makes a Midwest Thanksgiving, you may ask? All of the classics are present, plus a few surprising favorites that, in my house, no holiday is complete without. We think beyond the turkey, sometimes skip mashed potatoes for a cheesy casserole, and have to be careful not to fill up on all the rolls (butter and honey better be on the table). 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Budgeting, filling out tax forms together, managing family dynamics, and standing in line at city hall: not sexy. Not romantic. Alas, they are the mundane mechanics of even the most thrilling of married lives. Soon after a ring is on the finger, many couples are now discussing prenups—and it’s a topic that brings up unglamorous realities.

No, the administrative process of a prenup isn’t inherently romantic, and let’s not pretend it is. But what it does for the relationship—laying everything bare with radical honesty—is deeply romantic.

In a recent development, “I think navigating something that’s challenging in a relationship and coming out of it aligned is romantic, sexy, and empowering,” indicates Ashley Hesseltine. The co-host of Girls Gotta Eat spoke openly about choosing to have a prenuptial agreement with her now husband. “But I will not lie. The process of a prenup is inherently annoying, unsexy, and invasive. And it’s admin.”.

Sources indicate that wedding planning has a way of sweeping us up into a whirlwind of floral arrangements, seating charts, and linen swatches. Conversations about money, family expectations, and core values naturally come to the forefront next to celebrations.

In a recent development, luxury wedding planner JoAnn Gregoli agrees that pausing and zooming out to address a prenuptial agreement and the structural foundation of your partnership before you even start picking a venue makes the whole planning process all the more clear. “Marriage isn’t only about romance; it’s also about finances, property, obligations, and decision-making,” she claims. “When a couple confronts the subject together, they feel more like they’re entering the marriage as a team and not as a dictatorship.”.

In a recent development, you’ve likely already experienced that deep feeling of intimacy with your partner after an exceptionally vulnerable conversation with them. This is just like that. Afterwards, wedding planning transforms from a period of financial tension into one of deep alignment.

In a recent development, it helps, but there’s no requirement to execute a 30-page legal document to reap the emotional rewards of the prenup talk. Some value lies in the vulnerability required to have the conversation at all.

Therapist and author Israa Nasir notes that money remains one of the ultimate taboos in modern relationships, often carrying hidden emotional baggage. “Constructive and supportive conversations can reveal parts of yourself that you otherwise might not—deeper insecurities, past experiences with financial trauma, childhood scarcity, and your relationship with money,” she says. “If your partner doesn’t understand why you behave a certain way about money, it’s harder for them to have empathy for you.”.

In a recent development, it may feel like you’re setting up transactional boundaries or betting against your longevity. But in essence, it’s an exercise in radical honesty. Approaching your partner with curiosity rather than judgment is a quick way to turn a wobbly topic fraught with anxiety into a brick in your foundation.

In a recent development, nobody’s excited about asking their partner about student loans or retirement accounts. It may feel daunting. That’s completely normal.

Recent findings suggest that start small, and don’t put the pressure on this having to be one significant conversation. The first chat can just be about getting their thoughts on prenups in general. Then, you can talk about your thoughts on how you want to manage finances in your relationship. Finally, when you’re ready, you can start diving into assets and what each person wants to walk away with.

It has been revealed that the time-old advice of there being no such thing as too much communication stands here. You can even talk about how you want to enter this conversation in a way that might make both of you feel the most comfortable. Agree to enter the discussion with empathy, zero judgment, and positive intent.

Remind yourself that you can frame this discussion around shared goals and mutual care.

Here are a couple of conversation starters:.

I’m fairly certain nobody gets married to get divorced. If it does happen, state laws dictate what happens to you both. Letting state statutes dictate your shared destiny? Not romantic. An act of mutual protection? Maybe even chivalrous.

Family and divorce mediator Aswini Puvitharan highlights how modern prenups are moving away from traditional adversarial mindsets. “Prenups are often introduced as ‘How do I protect what’s mine?’ but the better starting point is ‘What would fairness and financial security look like for both of us?’ The more thoughtful prenups today reflect deep care—providing housing, financial support, or protecting someone who takes a career break to raise children.”.

Industry observers note that protection from potential bitterness or future legal chaos is inherently loving. “It should feel like you and your partner against the prenup, not you and your partner against each other,” notes Hesseltine. “It’s an insurance policy you’re probably never going to use, and if you were strong enough to figure this out together in a healthy way, chances are you’ll never need it.”.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

As an avid baker, I've been waiting for such a sturdy set.

Industry observers note that our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Serious bakers will appreciate the hefty, high-quality materials in this 6-piece set. It's also gloriously nonstick.

In a recent development, when I got married a few years ago, I put a cohesive bakeware set on my registry to replace years of mismatched Goodwill finds. While it worked well for a few months, within a year it began to show serious signs of wear and tear. Baked-on grease stains, rust spots and even warping had me in the market for a upcoming bakeware set much sooner than I expected.

So, when I heard that my favorite cookware brand was releasing a bakeware set promising a sturdy, nonstick experience, I jumped at the chance to test it. Here’s everything you need to know about the new HexClad bakeware line, including my honest thoughts after two months of testing.

HexClad’s newly introduced hybrid bakeware set features six core pieces:.

It merges the benefits of stainless steel and nonstick into one easy-to-clean package. HexClad’s “hybrid technology” combines hexagonal steel peaks with nonstick valleys to improve heat circulation and release after baking. In other words, this bakeware browns your food evenly without it sticking to the pan.

Other features include ergonomic handles and a 2.5mm tri-ply construction to prevent warping. It’s also oven-safe up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit and dishwasher-safe. You can even use your favorite metal spatula or tongs without scratching the surface. And, like all HexClad cookware, it comes with a lifetime warranty against manufacturer’s defects.

It has been revealed that I’ll admit: I’m already a big fan of HexClad. I reach for the brand’s skillets and knives daily, and I’ve hoped for years that they would release a bakeware line.

So, when the offer to test the new set landed in my inbox, I couldn’t say no. But would it live up to the hype I’d built up in my head? I put all six pieces through the paces for two months to find out.

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

It has been revealed that like all HexClad products I’ve tried, the bakeware packaging experience is impeccable. The set arrived securely in one big box, separated with foam. Each piece was also wrapped in a protective dust bag, which is a nice touch.

Immediately, I was awed by the construction of these pans. Just by touch, I could tell they were high quality. I grabbed my food scale to compare the weight of the HexClad pans to my go-to carbon steel pans. The HexClad options weighed more than twice as much as my existing bakeware. Talk about heft!

Now, some folks might not appreciate that extra weight—especially since the pans get even heavier when full of food. But as someone who often replaces her bakeware every few years due to warping or rusting, I’m excited for a sturdier option. I hope this is the last set of bakeware I ever need to order.

As a final step, I washed each piece and got ready to bake!

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

It has been revealed that one of my favorite things to make with sourdough discard is a big loaf of focaccia bread, so that was a natural first test in the 13×9 HexClad pan. Focaccia dough is sticky, but a generous coating of olive oil helps prevent it from gluing to the pan. Still, after proofing and baking my bread as usual, I was impressed that the final product pulled slightly away from the pan’s edges, making it slide out with complete ease. The bottom and edges got nice and toasty brown, too.

Sources indicate that A few nights later, I used the same focaccia dough to make a focaccia pizza. Same sticky dough, made even stickier with tomato sauce, cheese and toppings. Plus, since it’s such a rich dish, I cut back on the amount of olive oil I used. Despite all the add-ons, this focaccia baked and released from the pan just as beautifully as the first loaf.

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

Next, I made a chocolate layer cake with the 9-inch round cake pans. Now, I’m typically a ride-or-die parchment paper user. I find cutting out perfectly sized parchment circles a tedious task, but it’s worthwhile insurance against my cakes sticking. But to truly put the HexClad pans’ nonstick properties to the test, I skipped adding parchment and simply greased my pans with a little butter and flour.

After baking and 10 minutes of cooling came the moment of truth: Would it stick? Luckily, no! Both cakes released with minimal effort. I simply ran a butter knife around the rim of the cake before using the cooling rack to flip ’em out. It’s a good thing, too, because this was my dad’s birthday cake!

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

Recent findings suggest that my nonstick tests continued with the 8×8 square pan when I whipped up a batch of candy bar blondies. These blondies used an assortment of leftover Halloween candy, so I thought for sure the caramel ooze from a Baby Ruth bar would cause some concerns. But nope! Even without parchment paper, treats slipped right out of the pan.

But how does HexClad bakeware perform with healthier treats? For one final test, I baked a completely made-up “brownie” recipe with pumpkin seed butter, applesauce, molasses and cocoa. It was a gooey, chocolaty mess by the time I put it in the pan, yet it baked and released beautifully.

Finally, I put the baking sheet to the test.

Now, I already own the HexClad pizza steel, which I use almost daily. It’s my go-to for everything from frozen pizza to galettes to roasted broccoli, and I find that it works even better than an air fryer to yield crisp, golden brown bakes. I’ve noted on many occasions that it’s my all-time favorite piece of bakeware, especially for savory foods.

According to recent reports, both the pizza steel and baking sheet utilize HexClad’s tri-ply construction with an aluminum core and TerraBond nonstick coating. The former is a jet black colorway, while the baking sheet is gray.

Industry observers note that across the board, I found the baking sheet could handle every task I threw its way—including roasting a spaghetti squash. Oftentimes, I find myself scrubbing for what feels like days after roasting squash and scouring off that sticky, burnt-on residue. The HexClad pan cleaned with a simple swipe from a damp paper towel.

According to recent reports, during testing, I found the bottoms and handles of the HexClad bakeware smudged a bit. After all, it is made of stainless steel. This didn’t bother me, and it was easy to clean by handwashing and drying it immediately. Over time, I may need to use a more abrasive regimen to clean stainless steel.

Recent findings suggest that while the HexClad pans are very sturdy, you should still let them fully cool before washing. Don’t throw a hot pan directly in the sink. The pans are also dishwasher-safe, though handwashing is recommended. (And honestly, so easy thanks to the nonstick coating.).

Sources indicate that across the board, I’m impressed with the newly introduced HexClad bakeware line. I hope we see even more pieces in the future, like a muffin tin and loaf pan. Only time will tell exactly how it holds up, but from what I’ve experienced so far, this set really is designed to last a lifetime. (And I’ll be continuing to long-term test the set, and upgrade this review accordingly.).

It has been revealed that ready to take your bakes to the next level? This all-in-one set is great for beginners and pros alike.

Sources indicate that you can shop the full 6-piece bakeware set on the HexClad website for $399. Select styles, like 2-pack sets of small and medium baking sheets, are also available.

9 Best Coffee Subscriptions, Reviewed & Reordered (2026)

📅 23 Sep 2021 | ⏱️ 35 min read (7055 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~35 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s nothing worse than dragging myself out of bed only to realize I’ve run out of coffee beans.
  • Industry observers note that whether you’re a third-wave coffee nerd looking to try a newly introduced craft roaster or a decaf drinker on the hunt for some actually good decaffeinated beans, there’s a subscription for you.
  • I know coffee preferences can be wide-ranging, which is why my team and I have scoured the earth for subscriptions that offer tailored picks for different kinds of coffee lovers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s nothing worse than dragging myself out of bed only to realize I’ve run out of coffee beans. That’s where coffee subscriptions come in. But the best services will do more than guarantee you’ll have a consistent supply of freshly roasted coffee—they also let you explore the vast world of coffee. They’re how I’ve discovered some of my favorite roasters, tried single-origins I never would have found on my own, and figured out exactly what I like and don’t like in a cup.

Industry observers note that whether you’re a third-wave coffee nerd looking to try a newly introduced craft roaster or a decaf drinker on the hunt for some actually good decaffeinated beans, there’s a subscription for you. After five years of testing, Trade is our top pick—but depending on what kind of coffee you like, I have plenty of other recommendations.

I know coffee preferences can be wide-ranging, which is why my team and I have scoured the earth for subscriptions that offer tailored picks for different kinds of coffee lovers. To date, we’ve tested nearly two dozen options and recommend the following wholeheartedly.

New in this update: BA editors have been trying out some new deliveries, including some we’re loving from Methodical in Greenville, SC, and Fellow’s Drops program.

Trade is a multi-roaster subscription that sources coffee from independent roasters all over the country. It's great for someone looking for great specialty coffee with an interest in trying a number of different roasters and different roasting styles.

Recent findings suggest that tester: Chris Morocco, food director This was the easiest subscription I have ever set up, and Trade did such a good job of hitting my preferences right in their sweet spot: medium roast, medium body, medium fruit…just medium all around. I have gotten stuck in the past, tasting the same coffees or coffee styles over and over, and after just two bags, I could tell this would be different.

I set up an order for one 12-oz. bag of whole beans every two weeks. The first bag was Atomic Roasters Space Cadet out of Peabody, MA, and my second bag was Sparrows Coffee, Harmony Series All Seasons Blend from Grand Rapids, MI. I loved the Sparrows bag because it had just enough roast to feel pleasantly dense and weighty on my palate, yet with enough fruit, brightness, and acid to feel lively. When I clicked the box for “medium roast” coffee, this is exactly what I had in mind. I only do pour-over at home, and this was awesome in my Hario V60 coffee dripper.

Recently, senior shopping editor Olivia Tarantino tried Rarities, Trade’s newest program. It’s invite-only, with a rotating lineup of coffees that roasters make as experiments or passion projects. Each coffee is roasted and shipped to order, in batches of a few hundred bags at most. Trade provides detailed instructions direct from the roaster about how to best prepare your beans to get the optimal flavor extraction. She enjoyed an extended fermentation Chiroso variety that had complex acidity of citrus fruits and a slight savory flavor. We haven’t seen anything like Rarities from a subscription service, so serious coffee drinkers should jump on it.

The bottom line: There is a lot of great coffee in the world, but finding it and getting it right when you want it can be a challenge. Trade takes care of that for you, making this subscription absolutely worth it.

If you’re the kind of person who’s always ordering the fun new seasonal pour-over option at your local craft coffee shop, or who hunts down rare bean varietals like it’s your job, Podium Coffee Club’s Podium Platinum is the coffee subscription for you. Founded in 2023, Podium is a relatively new kid on the block in the world of coffee subs. The concept? A subscription service that solely sends out coffees that have stood on the podium (hence the name) at a major US coffee competition. The brand’s Podium Platinum subscription focuses on coffees that are unique and experimental in some way, be it flavor-wise, varietal-wise, or through the processing technique used.

In a recent development, testers: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor, and Alaina Chou, commerce writer In the two months we’ve tested this service, we’ve received two bags of coffee that have lived up to that claim. The first bag was a light roast from Royal Flamingo Coffee, a micro-roaster based in Columbus, Ohio. The beans, grown in Colombia, were made using the Black Honey process and mossto lactic fermentation, which you can read more about on Podium’s website. The notes of blueberries, white chocolate, and florals definitely came through in the brewed coffee in both smell and taste, though not too aggressively. We quite enjoyed this one.

It has been revealed that the next coffee hailed from Wonderstate Coffee in Wisconsin and claimed notes of gummy bear, melon, and cooked berries. That might seem like a crazy flavor profile for a bag of coffee, but the brewed stuff was subtle and highly drinkable.

Sources indicate that the bottom line: This is a great coffee subscription to get if you’re looking to explore, nerd out on coffee-making processes, or discover award-winning roasters from across the country. Note that Podium also offers a less expensive Podium Gold subscription option, which does not get you the same unique selection that the Platinum offers.

If you’re a curious coffee connoisseur looking to try single-origin coffee from around the world while directly supporting fair trade and sustainable practices, Atlas is the subscription service for you. Every month, you’ll get a bag of single-origin coffee from a different country that comes with an ID card detailing sourcing information and tasting notes.

Tester: Kelly Janke, former director of culinary production The ordering process was easy. It asked me a few questions about my preferences in roast level, brewing type, and coffee quantity, with options ranging from a half bag to four bags per month. The shipping did seem to take longer than I expected, which was my main qualm with the service.

The beans I received in my first month were medium roast from Rwanda. I really enjoyed the cards that came in the box with tasting notes and information on the growing region. I had chosen two bags per month because I drink a fair amount of coffee, but it’s worth noting that this meant I received two of the same exact coffee (which wasn’t clear at the time of ordering—I had assumed they would be different). I ground the beans in my Oxo burr coffee grinder to a medium grind and brewed them in a Chemex with a metal reusable filter using a 1:16 coffee-to-water ratio. The coffee definitely tasted on the darker side of a medium with notes of grape, red apple, and roasted almonds.

The bottom line: I love to try newly introduced coffee varieties and appreciate the difference; if you feel similarly, then Atlas is a great option for you.

It has been revealed that if you’ve been reading all of this as a decaf drinker, we have good news for you: there are also some great decaf coffee subscriptions out there, including Swiss Water. This subscription offers a rotating selection of decaf coffees from roasters all across the US, all of which have gone through the Swiss Water process, a chemical-free decaffeination technique that you can read more about here. Note that Swiss Water presently only offers whole bean coffees, so you’ll need to grind your own beans if you decide to try it out.

In a recent development, tester: Alaina Chou I opted for biweekly shipments, though Swiss Water also offers weekly, monthly, and bimonthly. The first coffee I received was from Manzanita Roasting Manufacturer, based in San Diego. There was no informational card included, so all I really gathered about the coffee was that it was from Guatemala and had notes of berries and chocolate, which it did. For a decaf brew, I was impressed by the quality and nuance of the flavor. The same can be stated for the second bag of beans I received, which was a blend called Kick Back from South Carolina–based Barista Alley.

The bottom line: You won’t find the kind of customization and curation options here that you see in most of the other subscriptions on this list, but if you’re okay with trying out a range of decaf coffees and aren’t married to one particular roast level or flavor profile, this service will work for you.

Of every coffee subscription we’ve ever tried, this one is unique. Most coffee beans, even if freshly roasted, are stored as green beans for months. Origin Roasted beans hit the roaster almost immediately after harvest and get shipped out right after that. Truly, they are the freshest coffee beans you can get without picking them yourself. It’s a subjective call as to whether that makes the flavor "better," but it makes it different.

In a recent development, tester: Noah Kaufman Fruity or chocolate tasting notes that are present in beans that sit green are massively accentuated with Origin Roasted beans. If a flavorful cup of coffee is what you’re after, these beans are as flavorful as they come. The brand’s commitment to roasting at the beans’ origin has the added effect of bringing more coffee roasting work and expertise to countries of origin; roasting for most American coffees happens in the United States.

Industry observers note that the ordering process is straightforward because there are no choices for you to make. Just give them your address and credit card number, and the coffee will be on its way to you at the end of each month. The manufacturer only sends the beans it is harvesting that month, which come from a single farm somewhere in Central or South America. The locations are limited to ensure that Origin Roasted can actually get the beans to your door while they’re as fresh as they’re supposed to be.

I got beans from all over Central and South America: Guatemala, Nicaragua, Panama, Colombia, Peru, and Brazil. Each coffee was entirely unlike the one that came before it. Shipments only get sent out on the 28th of every month, so I was limited to one bag per month.

It has been revealed that the bottom line: Because of the harvest and roast process, this really is a boutique product, so you can’t order en masse the way you can with larger roasters. I don’t think it makes sense to identify my favorite beans here because you, dear reader, are not guaranteed to get them anyway. What you are guaranteed to get are incredibly cool coffees.

Industry observers note that we are always on the hunt for roasters and subscriptions we haven’t tried. These are the ones that have landed in our grinders recently that we’re loving.

Sources indicate that if you're into the idea of coffee drinking as a ritualistic ~experience~, Folk Coffee Club is for you. Founded by a Q-Grader, a.k.a. a sommelier for the coffee world, Folk specializes in rare coffees that score at least 86 points (in Q-Grader speak). Unlike many of the other coffee subscriptions on this list, Folk gives you zero options; instead, they'll send you one shipment every month with two expert-curated coffees.

Sources indicate that tester: Alaina Chou What really sets Folk apart, though, are the intentional extras they included with each shipment. Along with the two coffees, each month features a piece of art, a curated playlist, some thought starters, and a tasting guide that elevate the mundane ritual of coffee brewing and drinking into a full-blown experience you're encouraged to slow down and savor. The whole package, coffees included, is meant to draw on a unifying theme.

Folk's first shipment, Volume 00, was titled “Off Script,” and featured two Gesha coffees—a distinctive varietal that takes supreme care to grow. Each coffee tasted unlike any other I've had, one with notes of jasmine and caramelized peach, the other reminiscent of blood orange and dark chocolate. The whole thing was beautifully packaged and felt like a luxurious gift to receive, the thoughtful intention behind each component highly evident.

The bottom line: Think of Folk like a monthly ritual, complete with art, a playlist, and rare coffees you won't find anywhere else. If you're the type to linger over your morning cup, this one's worth every penny.

Sources indicate that there is no better proof point that the world of exquisitely roasted coffee beans has anchored itself absolutely everywhere than the Onyx Coffee Lab. Onyx was started by Jon and Andrea Allen (who would later become a U.S. barista champion) in Springdale, Arkansas, in the Ozarks, and as it has spread throughout the state, it has also become one of the most recognizable names in specialty coffee. Such is Onyx’s reputation that it’s bled over into other areas, landing the Rogers, Arkansas headquarters a nod as a James Beard Award finalist for the best bar program in America.

Tester: Noah Kaufman As for the coffee subscriptions themselves, they’re straightforward to set up: simply tick the box for quantity and the box for frequency. Onyx offers the reliable roaster’s choice option with a lot of interesting single origins and one-offs (I particularly liked a Rwandan washed coffee from Kanzu Station) that all include the most informative explainers I’ve ever seen attached to a bag of coffee. The cards include a breakdown of all the inputs that contribute to the cost, detailed brewing instructions for both pour-over and espresso, and an explanation of the fermentation and roasting process.

For people looking for more familiar flavors, Onyx has subscription options that combine a small amount of more adventurous beans like the Kanzu with its more familiar blends, letting curious drinkers dip their toes in something fresh. And for a more special experience, Onyx releases a small number of memberships to what it calls “Echelon” for monthly deliveries of its rarest coffee.

Contemporary Coffee Subscription.

It has been revealed that the Greenville, South Carolina roaster has grown now to have five cafes, a robust bakery and tea program, and some of the coolest, most beautiful branding in the coffee world. But it also has a wide range of blends and single-producer beans.

I first walked into Methodical’s café in Greenville in 2017 for a single origin pour-over, and at the time quick national shipping of fresh coffee was still in its early stages, so that stop didn’t end with me signing up for regular deliveries. But now the infrastructure is there and the coffee is great. Methodical sorts its coffee into three main buckets for three different types of coffee drinkers: classic (where you’ll find medium and dark roasts great for batch brewing and espresso), contemporary (where you’ll find medium roast coffees great for batch brewing or pour-over), and “avant-garde” (where you’ll find lighter roast coffees, sometimes fruity, sometimes tea-like, that are best enjoyed black).

Industry observers note that our editors have used every one of these coffee subscriptions in their homes over several months and some for years. We’ve made sure to try a variety of bean types where possible, and to try the beans with a variety of brewing methods to see how well they perform as espresso, pour-over, drip coffee, and French-pressed coffee.

Our editors are continually testing many of these services and constantly trying upcoming coffee subscriptions to keep this list updated as the market changes, so be sure to check back as we enhancement it often.

There are hundreds of coffee subscriptions out there, so we followed two guiding principles when selecting which subscriptions to test:.

A coffee’s freshness has a huge impact on its flavor once brewed, no matter if you’re using a fancy espresso machine or a simple French press. The best subscription services will guarantee freshly roasted beans, either roasted to order or within a week or so of shipping.

The other major factor in your coffee’s flavor is how recently the beans were ground. I’m a big advocate of ordering whole-bean coffee and grinding the beans just before brewing, so all of the options we tested offer that. (Of course, I know that many people may prefer the convenience of ground coffee. Most of the services below also offer that as an option, although my colleagues and I will continue to raise our eyebrows at you until you get a good coffee grinder.).

Tester: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor Best for: People who want high-quality coffee, but aren’t interested in choosing from a dizzying array of adventurous options.

According to recent reports, intelligentsia, out of Chicago, is one of the OG players in third-wave coffee (if you’re unfamiliar, "third wave" has a specific meaning, but is sometimes used as shorthand for a generation of coffee roasters deeply invested in quality, consistency, and unique flavors in coffee). Intelligentsia’s House Blend and Black Cat espresso roast have become staples at bakeries and coffee shops all over the country, and its subscription service gives you a regular supply of those two as well as its deeper catalog of different beans. There’s one single origin option, but the subscription itself is mostly based around Intelligentsia’s blends, which rotate seasonally.

This is a pretty simple, straightforward subscription. There is no quiz or process to determine what kind of coffee is “best for you”; rather, you just manually put in which subscription you want, choosing between the same blend (including espresso), rotating blends, or the roaster’s choice. You can also select how many times a month you want beans and how many bags you want per shipment. Changing to a different subscription is also quite easy. While you won’t find the same kind of personalized curation options as some of the other subscriptions on this list, Intelligentsia does offer one of the widest ranges of grind types if you aren’t getting whole bean coffee, running from the finest Turkish coffee grind to a super coarse (even coarser than cold brew) percolator grind.

I got “Intelligentsia's Choice” because I’m a sucker for single-origin beans (and have had the opportunity to try all their classic blends already). The beans came from some of the strongholds of international coffee production: Ethiopia and Nicaragua. Making a carafe of pour-over coffee a day, enough for two people or one me, I used about one bag every two weeks. The most noteworthy coffee to me was a very fruity natural process Ethiopian coffee. After testing it extensively, I can tell you that this is a reliable, relatively affordable subscription; the Intelligentsia Classics subscription is only $17 a bag. It would be worthwhile for anyone who wants quality but isn’t trying to be too adventurous with their morning coffee.

In a recent development, just to note, in 2015, Peet’s bought up a majority stake in Intelligentsia. I don’t think it has changed the quality of the coffee at all, but it is something worth being transparent about.

Tester: Carly Westerfield, associate manager of audience strategy Best for: Someone who likes high-quality beans and doesn’t know exactly what flavor they’re looking for, but might get overwhelmed by some of the multi-roaster options on this list.

In a recent development, counter Culture is a longtime favorite roaster of many a BA staffer (food director Chris Morocco included). It has storefronts in several major cities, and you can find Counter Culture’s coffee in stores across the country, but they also offer several subscription options online.

It has been revealed that I had a really easy time ordering the coffee. There aren’t endless options to choose from, which is nice because subscriptions like these can sometimes be a lot to manage. Because I wanted to see a variety of beans, there were only two: the Single-Origin Subscription and the Blend Box. I opted for the latter. As someone who’s often overwhelmed by choices, I always appreciate a curated shopping experience where there are fewer things to choose from and therefore fewer things to compare, contrast, and potentially have buyer’s remorse over. I did struggle a little to figure out how to end the subscription; Counter Culture makes that part a little trickier than everything else.

It has been revealed that this subscription sends two different blends (12-oz. bags) at a time at a frequency of your choosing. Options there ranged from every week to every eight weeks, and the ability to change this post-purchase was clear. The Blend Box subscription pulls from six blend options ranging from light to dark roast, plus any “seasonal blend’ they have available, so you will end up seeing the same beans after about four deliveries. Shipping was fast and the email communication from CC made it so I always knew when I was being charged and when the box would be shipped and delivered.

While trying out this subscription, I received four different coffee blends: Iridescent Winter Blend, Big Trouble, Fast Forward, and Forty-Six. At home, I use a Moccamaster Thermal Carafe Coffee Brewer and a Baratza Encore Coffee Grinder. With each of the blends I received, I was able to use the same measurements that I always use (9 g of coffee per 6 oz. of water) and found the coffee to be the right strength for me. Each blend has spot-on tasting notes provided as well. Overall, while the flavor profiles were totally different, none were overwhelmingly bitter or acidic—a big no-no in my book. These coffees all had a really well-rounded, almost creamy quality to them that actually resulted in me using way less half-and-half than I normally take in my coffee. By far my favorite blend is, sadly, the limited edition Iridescent Winter Blend. Big Trouble came in a close second.

This subscription is great for someone who likes high-quality beans but doesn’t know exactly what flavor they’re looking for—perhaps, for instance, a recent college grad who’s been drinking coffee for years but hasn’t had to buy it for their own home yet. The ability to pause or change how often the deliveries come also makes it nice for someone who might travel often or need to have more coffee on hand at random times (maybe they have frequent house guests?).

Tester: Maria Paz Mendez Hodes, director of creative development Best for: Eager-to-learn beginners.

Industry observers note that stumptown is a Portland, OR–based roaster that’s been around since 1999. It offers three subscription options: Roaster’s Choice, Blend Shuffle, and Favorite on Repeat. As a novice coffee brewer, I wished there were a little more elaboration on the differences between Roaster’s Choice and Blend Shuffle. In the end I opted for the Roaster’s Choice, which promised to be a tour of seasonal, single-origin, and occasionally rare coffees, changing every two weeks.

In a recent development, I wasn’t 100% sure until the bag indicated up at my door that I was ordering whole beans versus ground coffee. To some that may be glaringly obvious, but just another reminder that the site did not seem aimed at rank beginners like me. From what I can tell, Stumptown subscriptions are all whole-bean-only. Beyond that, the ordering process was clear and easy! My first bag arrived three days after ordering, and the next one almost exactly on schedule.

A guilty confession: We keep breaking the Hario V60 carafe that I use to make pour-over, and I’ve gotten hooked on the extravagant convenience of bottled cold brew. The arrival of the Stumptown beans was exciting enough that we couldn’t wait for a replacement to arrive from Amazon, so we improvised by setting the dripper over a mason jar. Unglamorous setup aside, the first brew was an immediate reminder of the sense pleasures of the morning coffee ritual, dramatically amplified by using the fanciest beans I’d ever purchased. The freshness of the seasonal beans was obvious upon opening the package—they were lustrous and almost oily, with juicy notes that I’ve rarely detected in the supermarket brands near me. I don’t have a highly attuned coffee nose, but I could certainly taste distinct differences between the bags I received: light, bright fruit in the Montes de Oro from Costa Rica and deep caramel and spice in the Duramina from Ethiopia.

Industry observers note that there were blurbs on the back of each bag sketching details about the coffee producers (e.g., how long they’d partnered with Stumptown and some unique features of their agricultural operations). It’s a good initiation for an interested newbie, but I think a coffee enthusiast could still glean quite a bit from these brief details. The one addition I would have loved would have been a card in the box with some deeper insights connecting the tasting notes and flavors to the processes and places mentioned. While there were tasting notes on the website for “Pick of the Week,” the coffee described wasn’t one I had received—another argument for a card in the box.

Tester: Travis Rainey, staff photographer/visuals editor Best for: People who like a little personality in their morning coffee.

According to recent reports, I was tempted to choose a curveball and select the espresso subscription, but opted for a more American coffee experience this time. I chose to test the Curated Single Origin subscription, which sends you a different single-origin coffee bean each week. The first bag of beans I received was from Concepción Huista, just north of Huehuetenango in western Guatemala. It was a very light, almost delicate kind of coffee. I had to adjust the grinder setting to a finer coffee ground to make the coffee a little more bold. For the most part, I make coffee with a pour-over method. A fresh coffee arrives each week, so the next selection was from Abana Estate near Jimma in southwestern Ethiopia. This has been my favorite coffee to make so far. It's distinctive, spiced, but still goes down smooth. The third variety is Panangan Mata from Aceh on the northern tip of Sumatra in Indonesia. I’ve only had one cup yet, but it’s fruity, which is a fun surprise.

Sources indicate that in general, I’ve found that each Equator coffee has had a distinct personality, making this subscription ideal for people who want to have opinions about coffee—the beans here are the kind that sort of demand one of you. I also appreciate that the containers the coffee beans come in feature detailed, but succinct information on where the coffee is coming from.

Tester: Hana Asbrink, deputy food director Best for: Both novice and experienced coffee drinkers alike who want their coffee selections handled for them.

My ordering experience was straightforward. I chose the Roaster’s Choice Subscription, so I didn’t know what I’d be getting first. My first bag (Honduras San Francisco whole beans) had a roast date just three days before it arrived at my house, so you can’t get much fresher than that. I appreciated this first blind bean as I’m not sure I would have chosen it for myself based on my personal preferences. I used a medium grind on the whole beans for my drip coffee maker. I’m curious to see how I’ll enjoy it pulled in the significant boy coffee maker as an Americano.

Recent findings suggest that the bag touts tasting notes of strawberry, raspberry, and dark chocolate, which are spot-on. The first whiff gave me a fruit-and-nut chocolate bar, and the taste matches in a delicate way with a touch some floral undertones.

Tester: Carina Finn Best for: Best for someone with a high-end caffeine routine.

You can find a Blue Bottle café in most major cities—the brand makes a reliably great cup of coffee, whether you’re into fruity pour-overs or sophisticated seasonal lattes. Blue Bottle’s coffee subscription makes it easy to recreate that experience at home. It has around 10 different subscription options for things like instant espresso and matcha powders to rotating single-origin offerings and subscriptions tailored to specific roast level preferences.

Tester: Alaina Chou Best for: Someone looking for seasonality in their coffee.

According to recent reports, sightglass is a coffee-shop-slash-roaster based in San Francisco. They offer subscriptions for all of the coffees in their regular lineup if you find a fave you want to stick to, but we’d recommend trying out one of their rotating options to get a taste for all the brand has to offer. That leaves you with either the Blend Shuffle or the Seasonal Variety subscription. The ordering process is simple: Just select which subscription you want, how much coffee you want in each shipment (12 ounces, 2 pounds, or 5 pounds), what kind of grind you want, and how often you’d like to receive deliveries.

Sources indicate that one of the things I like about Sightglass, as opposed to some other coffee shop-roaster hybrids, is that they regularly introduce new single-origin coffees, which might feature in that seasonal subscription. You can also opt in to get notified about any new drops through the Sightglass Batches text-to-order service.

Sources indicate that I'm partial to Sightglass’s Blueboon blend. It's a medium roast with notes of milk chocolate, mandarin, and honeysuckle that I quite enjoy brewed as espresso and used in my morning iced latte. It’s beautifully balanced, and the components get changed seasonally to retain the right ratio of sweetness, body, and acidity.

Tester: Alaina Chou Best for: People who want to hone their coffee-tasting skills.

If you dream of being able to approach the coffee world with sommelier-like expertise but you aren’t quite there yet, a Driftaway coffee subscription will help. Driftaway is an immigrant-owned, woman-led roastery based in Brooklyn, NY, and it’s the only service we’ve tried that starts out with a blind tasting. When you go to place your first order, you’ll have the option to choose between light roast, medium, and dark roasts, or espresso (which each include two or three different 4-oz. bags of coffee to blind taste test), or opt for the Explorer Box, which includes five different coffees spanning all roast levels.

Recent findings suggest that if the tasting aspect of this service appeals to you, I’d recommend going with the Explorer Box option. Each initial Explorer Box comes with five mystery coffees, a wheel with flavor notes, a tasting form, and an envelope revealing the identities of your coffees. Driftaway offers weekly virtual tasting classes free of charge, but if you’d rather taste on your own time, they also have prerecorded tasting tutorials available on their website. Regardless of whether you opt for the Explorer Box or a roast-specific subscription, after your initial order, you’ll give feedback on which coffee you preferred in order to inform your future shipments. Many coffee companies even give you the option to send the farmer feedback, which I appreciated.

According to recent reports, along with the Explorer Box, I also tried out the espresso subscription. I was partial to the Burundi Turihamwe and Guatemala Ella blend, which was wonderfully nutty and had notes of milk chocolate and stone fruits. I loved being able to read more about the women farmers behind this blend and trace the story of the coffee from harvest to brewing, a feature that’s in keeping with Driftaway’s overall ethos.

Sources indicate that founded in 2015 in NYC's East Village, Coffee Project NY has grown from a single café into a full operation spanning retail, roasting, wholesale, and education. Owner Chi Sum Ngai is a certified Q grader and roasting championship competitor who personally oversees the roasting program, sourcing from small-scale cooperatives and family farms committed to improving conditions for workers.

It has been revealed that tester: Olivia Tarantino, senior commerce editor The subscription is straightforward: select the Roaster's Choice Single Origin Subscription and receive one to three 10-oz. bags one to two times a month. Coffee Project Upcoming York is not shy about its credentials; each bag arrives with tasting notes, farm sourcing, processing methods, and MASL (metres above sea level, which indicates the altitude at which beans were grown and profoundly impacts flavor). My standout was the Cabra Noir Wush Wush from the Competition Series, a runner-up at Mexico's prestigious AMCCE competition. Produced through anaerobic fermentation, I hand-ground the beans for a Hario pour-over and was met with such vivid guava notes that I double-checked the bag to make sure it wasn't a cofermentation. It wasn't. It was just that good.

Bottom line: Any coffee drinker will appreciate the expertly sourced beans, but this is a subscription where nerds can truly geek out, sampling rare cultivars and competition-level coffees from around the world.

Wonderstate Coffee (Single Origin).

Wonderstate Coffee Blend Shuffle).

Wonderstate Coffee (Roaster's Choice).

A certified B-Corporation with a fully solar-powered roastery, a transparent farmer payment model, and a novel profit-sharing model, Viroqua-based Wonderstate has gained a lot of goodwill for its business practices, but it also makes really good coffee.

It has been revealed that tester: Noah Kaufman Admittedly, this is a bit of a homer pick, as I have long thought Wonderstate to be the preeminent coffee roaster from my beloved home state of Wisconsin. But for those of you not lucky enough to be from Wisconsin, you should get to know them too. Twice named roaster of the year by Roast magazine (which is probably how it ended up as part of the Podium Coffee subscription), Wonderstate regularly has delicious, clean limited edition single origins—I like to get them as part of the single origin flight subscription. The subscriptions themselves come in a few varieties. The single-origin flight delivers three 100-gram packages of Wonderstate’s rarer coffees every two weeks. Roaster’s choice delivers a different single-origin coffee at an interval of your choosing. And the single coffee subscription gives you a regular delivery of the Wonderstate blend of your choosing, if you’re the type who wants more consistency of flavor in your morning cup.

It has been revealed that the bottom line: Wonderstate makes excellent coffee and runs an ethical business, which is a combination that's rarer than it should be. If you care about where your money goes as much as what's in your cup, this is the subscription for you.

Black & White Roasters (1-Bag Specialty Subscription).

Black & White Roasters (1-Bag Year Round Subscription).

If you find most black coffee off-putting, you might still love an unadulterated cup from Raleigh, North Carolina’s Black and White Coffee Roasters. Started by two American barista champions, Black and White are masters of the funky and fruity, with lots of experiments in co-fermented coffee (a process that uses actual fruit) and anaerobic fermented coffee (which produces very pronounced fruit notes).

Tester: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor It can be a very hands-off subscription. The only required information is whether you want one or two bags at a time and the frequency you need your coffee (anywhere between one and six weeks). Black and White will take care of the rest. If you do see a bag on their website you like, you can add it to your queue; otherwise, the team in North Carolina will select for you.

Every bag I received was of a funky variety, using ingredients like passion fruit, but they produce a number of more classic flavor profiles, which are available as part of their “year-round” subscription; the year-round is also about 20% cheaper than a subscription with the specialty bags.

It has been revealed that the bottom line: If you're drawn to funky, fruit-forward coffee but don't want to think too hard about what to order next, Black and White is the subscription for you. Just set your frequency and let the barista champions decide.

In a recent development, bean Box is focused on the “curation” experience. The service’s tasting team offers what they claim is the largest selection of specialty coffee online, with over 600 different brews in its rolodex. The selection is sourced from dozens of small-batch, sustainably focused roasters from around the country—meaning you could likely go years without tasting coffee from the same roaster twice.

Sources indicate that tester: Dan Siegel, head of video Starting my subscription was exceptionally easy and clear. I appreciated the option to tailor the subscription to my own tastes: Bean Box asked me to choose among Light & Bright, Medium & Cozy, Dark & Toasty, Espresso, or Decaf. For this run, I selected the Curators' Choice option, marketed as the curation team’s seasonal favorites and a mix of new and old coffees. There is an app available to manage subscriptions and read lengthy details on each roaster or track the origin of your beans.

Industry observers note that this subscription was not designed to save me money on coffee; this is for enthusiasts. My first bag from “Gimme! Coffee,” out of Ithaca, NY, hit hard on the Bean Box mission: The roaster is employee-owned, shipping fair trade beans from Coopfam, Brazil’s first certified fair trade coffee grower. This was a standout for any time of day as a medium-bodied brew, subtly sweet with virtually no bitterness or acidity via my automatic OXO 8-cup machine or my Hario V60 pour-over. My second bag, La Cumbre from Little City in Austin, was a bit too bright and fruity for my taste, advertising caramel, mango, and green apple tasting notes—but this was the path I chose with the Curator’s Choice option.

It has been revealed that the bottom line: If you have the means, get the beans. I would keep this going for years if money were no object. The money seems to be going toward roasters that align with my values. One of my values is delicious coffee. But also treating workers at every stop along the way like human beings.

In a recent development, if receiving personalized coffee picks from a catalogue of nearly 600 coffees from 60 different roasters sounds like your cup of tea (or, rather, joe), then I will point you toward MistoBox. I found a lot to love about this service after testing it for several months, particularly the way Misto tailored its selections to me and my taste.

Tester: Alaina Chou, commerce writer The ordering process starts with a quiz covering your preferences: how you take your coffee, roast level, whole or ground beans, and frequency. But what sets MistoBox apart is what comes after: a second, more detailed quiz where you share how you brew, how you grind, and any other specifics to help the team dial in your order. The whole process feels genuinely personal, and that expert-curated aspect is, to me, the other major perk that makes a subscription worth it in the first place.

I’ve loved every coffee MistoBox has sent me so far. The first shipment was the Roma Espresso Blend from Parisi Artisan Coffee, which was aptly described as having notes of milk chocolate, almond, and honeysuckle. I tend to drink espresso, most often with milk in a cappuccino made using my Breville Oracle Jet. The Roma blend, which MistoBox sent me based on that information, worked beautifully for this.

After you receive each coffee, you’ll have the chance to rate it out of five and leave any tasting notes, which you can share with your curators if you’d like. Coffees you’ve tried show up in a customer dashboard, as will your “Brew Queue,” a.k.a. the lineup of the next coffees coming to your door. These will appear as “MistoBox’s choice” by default, but if you loved a coffee you tried and want it again, or spy a coffee in their collection that you’d like to request, you can opt to add specific coffees to your queue as well. Anyone looking for some expert guidance in discovering new coffees from roasters all over the country will enjoy MistoBox.

The bottom line: MistoBox’s user-friendly interface and extensive feedback options make it a great choice for anyone looking for some expert guidance in discovering new coffees from roasters all over the country.

Are coffee subscriptions worth it?

Industry observers note that if you’re a frequent coffee drinker, the answer is probably yes. Whether you have a favorite blend you find yourself buying on repeat or you’re eager to try new beans and hone your tasting skills, a coffee subscription will make your life easier and may even save you some money. If you’re presently buying a bag of beans every few weeks at your local coffee shop or grocery store, that bag could potentially be cheaper when bought on subscription—and you’ll get the added convenience of never needing to worry about restocking your stash.

How do coffee subscriptions work?

Sources indicate that at the most basic level, a coffee subscription works much like any other subscription service: You select a quantity and frequency, and lo and behold, a bag of freshly roasted coffee highlights up at your doorstep every one to four weeks, depending what you chose. But no one wants to come home from vacation to a pile of beans that are past their prime, only to receive another package the following day. So these coffee subscriptions make it easy to put your coffee deliveries on hold, or cancel them altogether. Some also offer personalization in the form of quizzes or feedback forms, so you can know you're getting a curated selection that’s tailored specifically to your tastes.

How much coffee should you order?

Many of the subscriptions on this list will let you customize your delivery frequency and bag quantity to best accommodate your household size and coffee drinking habits. Ideally, you’ll want to hit a sweet spot where you're using up nearly all of your beans by the time the next shipment comes. To figure out the right amount of coffee for you, you’ll need to do a little math:.

If instant coffee is more your speed, we don’t blame you—it’s hard to beat the convenience. And while instant coffee has historically gotten a bad wrap from third-wave coffee nerds and espresso heads everywhere, you’d be surprised what innovations have been made in the space in recent years. After tasting a whopping 40, we found a range of great-tasting options that would impress even the most seasoned coffee pro. Head this way for our review of all the best instant coffees and espressos money can buy.

Now that you’ve read all about the best coffee subscription services out there, it’s time to upgrade that old drip coffee machine or invest in a new espresso setup.

Is Pink Turkey Safe to Eat?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (833 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • I’ll never forget the Thanksgiving when I was convinced I’d ruined the holiday for everyone.
  • According to recent reports, imagine my surprise and horror when I carved that gorgeously browned roast turkey and discovered it was pink inside.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

According to recent reports, pink turkey doesn't necessarily mean your Thanksgiving feast is ruined. Here's how to know if your bird is safe to eat so you can stay calm and turkey on.

I’ll never forget the Thanksgiving when I was convinced I’d ruined the holiday for everyone. I wasn’t an experienced cook at the time, and it was one of my first attempts at making a Thanksgiving turkey. I used a helpful guide for how long to cook a turkey and even invested in a meat thermometer to be sure it reached at least 165°F. It looked great, and I was so proud!

According to recent reports, imagine my surprise and horror when I carved that gorgeously browned roast turkey and discovered it was pink inside. I was so nervous my guests would assume the turkey was undercooked. I didn’t know then that pink turkey can be perfectly safe to eat—as long as it’s cooked to that vital internal temperature.

Cooked turkey can look pink for a few reasons that have nothing to do with doneness, including the age of the bird, how it’s prepared and natural pigmentation.

Recent findings suggest that “Poultry naturally can have a pink hue,” claims Heidi Diestel of turkey farm Diestel Family Ranch in Sonora, California. “The legs and thighs have more of the natural pigments that give meat its darker color. Those pigments, along with changes that happen during cooking, can leave some pink even when the turkey is fully cooked.”.

It has been revealed that the pigments Heidi refers to are proteins called myoglobin and cytochrome c. The more of these proteins the meat has, the darker it will be. Older animals tend to have more proteins, and therefore darker pigmentation, as do any regularly exercised muscles. That explains why leg meat is darker than breast meat, as turkeys spend the bulk of their days walking and running.

Sources indicate that cooking can also cause a chemical reaction with these proteins that contributes to a pink color. Smoked turkey often stays pink from the reaction of the meat to the smoke inside the grill or smoker, but even oven-roasted turkey can have a pinkish hue. Myoglobin usually turns white during the cooking process, but cytochrome c is more resistant to heat and can maintain a pink blush.

Grace Natoli Sheldon for Taste of Home.

Using a meat thermometer is the best way to know if your turkey is safe to eat.

Poultry is considered safe to eat when it meets a cooking temperature of at least 165°. However, the Taste of Home Test Kitchen recommends cooking the leg and thigh meat to 170° for the best texture. For stuffed turkeys, don’t forget to take the temperature of the stuffing as well, which should reach at least 165° when the thermometer is inserted in the center of the stuffing.

If your turkey comes embedded with a round plastic doneness indicator that pops when the turkey is ready, don’t use that as an absolute; they are notoriously inaccurate.

To check if the turkey is done, insert the thermometer in a thick, meaty area, making sure the tip doesn’t touch any bones (bone will show a higher temperature).

If you’re using a probe thermometer that you insert before cooking, double-check its position once the turkey has been cooking for a while. Meat contracts as it cooks, so it may no longer be in the best spot.

If any part of your turkey is below 165°, you should continue cooking the turkey until all parts reach a safe temperature. It’s common for the thermometer to register different temperatures in different areas, since white meat cooks at a faster rate than dark meat. Don’t be tempted to cut off the parts that aren’t ready and return only them to the oven. It’ll increase the risk that undercooked juices will run onto your cutting board and contaminate the properly cooked turkey.

Industry observers note that if the legs and thighs aren’t done but the breast is, I like to baste the white meat and loosely tent it with foil to try and lock in as much moisture as possible. If the dark meat is ready but the breast needs more time, there’s no need to sweat it. Dark meat has enough natural fat and moisture that it won’t become dry with a little extra time in the oven.

Sources indicate that you should never knowingly eat undercooked turkey. According to the CDC, undercooked turkey can contain harmful bacteria, like Salmonella, Clostridium perfringens or Campylobacter, that can cause foodborne illnesses.

In a recent development, there’s also a risk of bacteria if the turkey isn’t thawed or prepared correctly. Give yourself plenty of time to thaw a frozen turkey, either in the refrigerator or in a cold water bath. Also, make sure to keep the counter or cutting board where you’re prepping the turkey clean and sanitized before and after handling the raw bird.

Chick-fil-A has built its reputation around a simple, flavorful chicken sandwich that doesn’t need much to stand out. Popeyes, meanwhile, practically broke the internet when it introduced its now-famous chicken sandwich in 2019, sparking a fast food frenzy.

I ordered each chain’s original chicken sandwich to compare flavor, texture, juiciness, and overall balance. Both have their strengths, but only one can move on as my favorite.

Chick-fil-A’s Original Chicken Sandwich keeps things simple with a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, and a toasted bun.

Sources indicate that chick-fil-A’s chicken is so recognizable for a reason. The seasoning and brine give the fillet a savory, slightly tangy flavor that’s hard to beat, while the crispy breading contrasts nicely with the juicy chicken. Industry observers note that my biggest complaint is that I wanted a little more from the sandwich. Compared to other fast food chicken sandwiches I’ve tried, many of which come with some type of sauce, Chick-fil-A’s original feels a bit plain. The chicken has enough flavor to stand on its own, but I think a little mayo or another sauce would have made the overall sandwich even better.

Still, there’s something to be remarked for a chicken sandwich that relies almost entirely on the quality and flavor of the chicken itself.

According to recent reports, popeyes’ Classic Chicken Sandwich features a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, mayo, and a toasted brioche bun. The sandwich that practically broke the internet when it debuted in 2019 still lives up to the hype.

I’ve had this sandwich before where the chicken was slightly dry in spots, but thankfully that wasn’t the case this time. The fillet was juicy, flavorful, and incredibly well-seasoned. The breading had a satisfying crunch, and the bold, savory flavor made me want to keep going back for another bite.

It has been revealed that the mayo was another important part of the sandwich, adding a tangy creaminess that complemented the chicken without overpowering it. Paired with the crisp pickles, it helped balance out the richness of the fried fillet.

I also really appreciated the proportions. The soft brioche bun held everything together without overwhelming the chicken, and each bite had a good balance of meat, breading, sauce, and pickles.

Sources indicate that while Popeyes might not always deliver the most consistently juicy chicken, everything came together particularly well during this taste test. Between the seasoning, crispy breading, and well-balanced toppings, it’s easy to understand why this sandwich became such a phenomenon in the first place.

Popeyes already managed to beat KFC in my previous comparison, and after going up against Chick-fil-A, it’s keeping its winning streak alive.

According to recent reports, chick-fil-A arguably has the more distinctive chicken flavor, thanks to its savory, slightly tangy seasoning. But when I’m ordering a chicken sandwich, I want the entire thing to work together, and that’s where Popeyes has the advantage.

Chick-fil-A is still a great option, especially if you prefer a simpler sandwich that lets the chicken do most of the work. But after trying both, Popeyes delivered the better overall experience. With two wins under its belt, Popeyes is proving to be a pretty tough sandwich to beat.

Instead of serving alongside crudités, toss this sauce with hot long pasta like linguine or spaghetti. No extra vegetables or protein needed, but I wouldn’t kick a salad with beans and bitter-slanting greens (kale, radicchio) off the table.

More weeknight-friendly pasta dinners this way.

Industry News: Which Thanksgiving Foods Belong in the Same Bite?

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that some Thanksgiving food combinations are obvious.
  • Industry observers note that for years, my kids refused to let any two foods touch on their plates.
  • In a recent development, of course, plenty of adults also have strong opinions about which Thanksgiving foods should mingle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Industry observers note that some Thanksgiving food combinations are obvious. Others might earn you some questioning looks at the dinner table.

Industry observers note that for years, my kids refused to let any two foods touch on their plates. I found this particularly maddening at Thanksgiving. There’s an entire table of food to fit onto a single plate and only so much room to negotiate separate territories for the mashed potatoes and green bean casserole! Thankfully, they’re a little more accommodating these days and, like me, have come to appreciate the occasional overlap between dishes.

In a recent development, of course, plenty of adults also have strong opinions about which Thanksgiving foods should mingle. There are those who insist on keeping every dish separate, those who permit a little gravy to stray onto the stuffing but draw the line at cranberry sauce, and those who deliberately assemble the perfect combination on every forkful. Then there’s always the unhinged relative who stirs the entire contents of their plate into a single, gravy-saturated mass and eats it with the serene confidence of someone who has never once questioned their choices.

Personally, I’m firmly in favor of combining foods, although I do believe a little discretion is in order. Thanksgiving dinner offers a wonderful assortment of rich, savory and tart flavors, and knowing which ones to bring together is part of what makes the meal so satisfying. There’s a culinary reason that cranberry sauce belongs alongside turkey, and that stuffing and mashed potatoes are particularly good together. And once you understand why those combinations work, you can start building some excellent bites of your own.

Sources indicate that absolutely. In fact, some of the most familiar food pairings are built around the idea that one ingredient can supply something another lacks. Think of a rich cut of meat served with a sharp, acidic sauce, or a creamy dish finished with something crisp. Neither component is necessarily lacking on its own, but the contrast makes the combination much more interesting.

Recent findings suggest that the same principle applies to Thanksgiving foods. Acidity helps balance richness, sweetness can temper salty or intensely savory flavors, and a change in texture can make a forkful more interesting. It’s not particularly complicated, but there’s a difference between understanding why two foods complement each other and simply hoping for the best.

Some combinations are simply better than others, though saying so at Thanksgiving dinner may invite more opinions than you bargained for.

Industry observers note that turkey and cranberry sauce: There’s a reason this pairing has endured for generations. Turkey, particularly the breast meat, is relatively mild, and the tartness of cranberry sauce gives it a welcome lift. It’s also an excellent remedy for turkey that’s spent a little too long in the oven, a situation that has befallen even the most conscientious Thanksgiving cooks.

In a recent development, mashed potatoes, stuffing and gravy: I consider this one of Thanksgiving’s greatest achievements. The smooth, buttery potatoes and herbaceous stuffing are excellent together, and a generous spoonful of gravy makes the whole arrangement even better. There’s nothing particularly subtle about it, but Thanksgiving dinner isn’t generally celebrated for its subtlety.

Recent findings suggest that sweet potatoes and turkey: The natural sweetness of roasted sweet potatoes makes a lovely contrast to savory turkey, particularly the richer dark meat. A traditional sweet potato casserole can work, too, although I draw the line somewhere around the marshmallow topping. I have nothing against marshmallows, but I prefer to encounter them after dinner.

In a recent development, green bean casserole and mashed potatoes: These are two of my Thanksgiving essentials, and I see no reason they shouldn’t share a fork. The creamy green beans and buttery potatoes are lovely together, but it’s the crispy fried onions that really make the combination work. That salty crunch is a welcome addition to the softer textures.

Turkey, stuffing and cranberry sauce: This is probably my favorite combo of the bunch. The savory turkey and seasoned stuffing are practically made for one another, while a little cranberry sauce cuts through the richness. It’s essentially a Thanksgiving leftover sandwich without the bread, although I wouldn’t object to adding a dinner roll to the equation.

According to recent reports, macaroni and cheese and cranberry sauce: I realize this combination may call my culinary credentials into question, but hear me out. Rich, creamy mac and cheese practically begs for something sharp and acidic to cut through it, and cranberry sauce does exactly that. It’s not so different from serving a sharp cheddar with fruit preserves on a charcuterie board, although I concede that putting cranberry sauce on macaroni and cheese is a considerably harder sell. But that’s half the fun of Thanksgiving dinner: discovering which combinations you’re willing to defend.

NASA's Voyager 1 mission forever changed our view of Jupiter

💡 Key Takeaways
